strengths: Clear formalization of what constitutes a 'good' training invariant (non-degeneracy, correctness, usefulness, compactness), grounding the empirical pipeline in a principled definition rather than ad hoc heuristics.

The WONDA pipeline (AST normalization + LLM-driven semantic simplification with mandatory re-verification) is a sensible, well-motivated approach to the data quality bottleneck identified in prior fine-tuning work (Wei et al., 2025), and the paper provides intuitive worked examples (Figs. 2-5) illustrating the transformation stages.

The ablation study (V0 vs V1 vs V2) convincingly isolates the contribution of normalization vs. LLM-based simplification, showing that normalization alone restores syntactic validity but LLM simplification is what drives the large gains in correctness/speedup/VBP.

The proposed VBP/VBS portfolio-based evaluation metric is a useful conceptual contribution that better reflects realistic deployment (parallel LLM + symbolic verifier) than naive sequential speedup metrics, and is a nice methodological point beyond the specific curation technique.

Consistent improvements are shown across three model scales (0.6B, 4B, 8B), and the fine-tuned 4B model achieves VBP comparable to GPT-OSS-120B, which is a meaningful demonstration that curated data can close much of the gap to much larger models at lower inference cost.
Reasonable reproducibility effort: prompts, algorithms, hyperparameters, and dataset/hardware details are provided in the appendix, and the paper states code/model/dataset release.
weaknesses: The evaluation set is small (123 hard instances) and results are averaged over only 3 runs with fairly large standard deviations (e.g., Qwen3-8B-V2 correctness 42.8±4.6%), making it hard to assess the statistical robustness of the reported gains, especially for the 'Solved' timeout-resolution counts which are reported as tiny per-run integers.

All experiments rely on a single backend verifier (UAutomizer) and a single benchmark source (SV-COMP/InvBench derived programs); generalization to other verifiers or program domains is left entirely to future work, limiting the demonstrated significance of the approach.

The framing that the 4B model 'approaches' GPT-5.2 undersells a fairly large remaining gap in raw correctness (44.4% vs 72.4%) and speedup rate (24.7% vs 37.1%); the VBP metric narrows this gap partly because both fail similarly often, and this nuance could be presented more critically rather than as a headline result.

The 'provable quality guarantees' language and the formal Propositions 4.1/4.3 are essentially restatements of construction-by-verification (any output that passes verifier checks is by definition correct) and add little beyond the empirical pipeline; describing this as a rigorous theoretical contribution somewhat overstates its novelty.

Key design choices (choice of Kimi K2 Thinking as the simplification LLM, N=4 candidates, verbosity threshold η) are not ablated or justified quantitatively, leaving open how sensitive the results are to these hyperparameters.

No comparison against alternative existing data-curation or filtering strategies from the literature (e.g., contrastive ranking as in iRank, or simple length/complexity filtering baselines); the only baselines are the pipeline's own intermediate stages (V0/V1) and untrained base models.

The central 'pedagogical value' / interpretability claim motivating the approach is not directly validated (e.g., via human judgment or downstream probing of whether simplified invariants actually teach transferable reasoning); the argument remains largely qualitative and illustrated only by cherry-picked examples.

No analysis of the failure/attrition rate of the LLM simplification step (e.g., what fraction of candidates are discarded for failing correctness/sufficiency checks), which would help assess the practical cost and reliability of the curation pipeline itself.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper identifies a plausible and underexplored issue (raw solver-generated invariants are structurally noisy/verbose and may not be 'learnable' targets) and formalizes desired properties of good training invariants (non-degeneracy, correctness, usefulness, compactness).

The WONDA pipeline is methodologically sound: AST-based normalization with simple, provably semantics-preserving rewrite rules, followed by LLM-driven simplification that is explicitly re-verified for correctness and sufficiency before being accepted as training data, ensuring the final curated dataset is sound by construction.

Thorough empirical evaluation across three model families (Qwen3 0.6B-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B) and multiple metrics (correctness, speedup rate, VBP, VBP_E2E), with an explicit ablation isolating the contribution of normalization (V1) versus LLM simplification (V2), showing consistent improvements from V0->V1->V2 across nearly all models and both easy/hard splits.
Good supplementary material: detailed prompts, algorithms, dataset statistics, hardware/verifier configuration, and hyperparameters are provided, supporting reproducibility.

The qualitative case study (Figure 5, cohendiv example) is a compelling illustration of how case-enumeration invariants are compressed into closed-form expressions, giving intuitive insight into why the method helps.

The comparisons against much larger off-the-shelf and frontier models (Qwen3-80B, GPT-OSS-120B, GPT-5.2) contextualize the practical value of small-model fine-tuning for a compute/cost-sensitive application.
weaknesses: Absolute performance remains modest even after fine-tuning: correctness rates on the hard split top out around 43-45% and speedup rates around 14-25%, considerably below GPT-5.2's 72.4%/37.1%; the paper's framing (e.g., 'matches GPT-5.2') rests heavily on the aggregate VBP_E2E metric, which is dampened by the parallel virtual-best-solver fallback to the baseline verifier and can mask substantial gaps in raw model capability (Rcorrect).

The 'provable quality guarantees' and soundness propositions (4.1, 4.3) are essentially restatements that verifier checks pass by construction; they do not add substantive theoretical depth beyond the empirical pipeline design, so the framing as a rigorous formal contribution may be overstated.

Evaluation is based on relatively small samples (n=123 hard instances, 3 runs), and reported differences between many model configurations have overlapping error bars (e.g., Qwen3-14B vs Qwen3-14B-V2 correctness 36.3±1.9 vs 43.4±4.9); no formal statistical significance testing is reported, making some comparative claims less conclusive.

The 'Solved' timeout-resolution numbers are very small in absolute count (e.g., 3-4 instances per run out of 20), so claims about WONDA-trained models resolving more baseline timeouts than GPT-5.2 rest on very thin evidence.

The method depends entirely on a single backend verifier (UAutomizer) for both raw invariant collection and quality grading, and timing-based grading (tv < tb) can be sensitive to machine/load noise; the paper acknowledges this as a limitation but does not empirically test robustness to using an alternative verifier or noisier timing conditions.

No direct comparison to iterative generate-and-verify baselines (Lemur, Loopy, ACInv) that are discussed in related work; since the paper claims one-shot and iterative approaches are complementary, an empirical comparison or combination would strengthen the significance claims.

The LLM simplification step uses a large model (Kimi K2 Thinking) to generate training data for smaller models; the paper does not discuss the cost/overhead of this data-generation step or potential distillation biases introduced by relying on a single large teacher model for semantic rewriting.

Generalizability beyond C/SV-COMP style benchmarks and the specific Hoare-logic verification setting used by InvBench is untested, limiting confidence in broader applicability of the curation approach.
